The Lee-Yang circle theorem places every zero of a ferromagnetic Ising partition polynomial on the unit circle. The arc condition, that every zero lie in the closed left half-plane, turns the circle theorem into a product formula for the characteristic function of the occupation count and makes it usable for local limit theorems. For the two-row periodic Ising torus we give the exact reflection factorization of the row transfer matrix, reduce the crossing at zeta = i to a real cubic, and identify the critical coupling a_c* = 0.8637850566870... as the unique root in (0,1) of an explicit octic. We prove that every a > a_c* satisfies the arc condition simultaneously for all circumferences, that no smaller coupling does, and that the finite thresholds approach a_c* at the rate C/n^2 with an explicit algebraic constant C. The factorization and the 2x2 threshold are formalized in Lean 4 against Mathlib; the zeta = i reduction, uniformity and rate are analysis-level.

item.title: Terrain-Surface-Area Cover from LiDAR: Inverse-Probability-Weighted Estimation and a Global Cramér-von Mises Lack-of-Fit Test
item.dc:creator: Marco Mandap
item.description:
Definitions of terrain area density, normalized surface measure, weighted Cramér-von Mises statistic, and their exact reductions and bounds are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Canopy cover is normally reported as a fraction of a horizontal map plane. When the domain of inference is the land surface, the appropriate target is the fraction of terrain surface area under canopy. We define this estimand on a C1 graph surface and show that it differs from vertical-projection cover by the planimetric covariance of cover with the area density, divided by the mean area density; the rumple index is a different quantity. A LiDAR pulse is recorded as a canopy return only when detection succeeds, so the naive return fraction estimates cover multiplied by the canopy detection probability. We study an inverse-probability-weighted estimator that uses that probability as the inclusion probability, and a weighted corner-averaged Cramér-von Mises lack-of-fit statistic for constant mean surface-area cover under independent canopy returns, calibrated by a parametric bootstrap. Synthetic validation on the flat plane and the Gaussian hill gives a naive bias near -0.40 and a weighted bias near 0.00; at 5000 pulses the test holds size at 0.02-0.06 across the simulated null cells and reaches power 0.79 under surface-uniform and 0.85 under plane-uniform sampling against broad slope-dependent cover, but only 0.12-0.13 against a compact hotspot. The definitions and their exact reductions are machine-checked in Lean 4. No field data yet.

item.title: Handling JAX
item.dc:creator: Oghenevwogaga Ebresafe, Daniel Zheng, Gordon Plotkin, Ningning Xie
item.description:
The jaxpr effect-handler calculus and the proofs that its handler-eliminating translation preserves typing and semantics are mechanized in Lean 4.
Languages that target hardware accelerators typically expose a restricted, first-order core without recursion or first-class functions, leaving programmers without a principled way to express computational effects. This paper presents a technique for compiling effect handlers to such a constrained target. We introduce a novel translation that statically eliminates effect handlers, and prove that it preserves both typing and semantics. Moreover, we address the challenges of integrating effect handlers with structured control flow, where continuations cannot be constructed statically. The calculus and all our results are fully mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant. Finally, we implement our design as a library for JAX, a Python domain-specific language for accelerator programming, and demonstrate its expressiveness through practical case studies.

item.title: Lemmas and Conjectures in Spectral Graph Theory
item.dc:creator: Tristan Cazenave
item.description:
An AI-generated pipeline formalizes spectral graph theory lemmas and 79,505 proved conjectures in Lean 4/Mathlib, including a 3,500-line Yang–Lu proof.
The corpus of Elie Duhamel and Tristan Cazenave \cite{dc} contains $305{,}755$ automatically generated conjectures relating spectral and metric invariants of connected graphs. A pipeline generated with Claude Code (numerical refutation, proof by the SMT solver z3 from a library of lemmas, discovery of new lemmas, formalisation in \lean 4/Mathlib) refuted $162{,}964$ conjectures and proved $117{,}390$ without any unproved hypothesis, of which $79{,}505$ are verified end to end in \lean{} for every connected graph. This document collects, with proofs written for mathematicians, the most interesting lemmas that were discovered and proved, the ten most useful lemmas, the ten hardest theorems, simpler proofs of known results (Bollobás–Erdős, Yang–Lu), and the unrefuted conjectures that we find most interesting. All the proofs are gathered in an archive

item.title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
item.dc:creator: Arpit Arora, Adam Holmes, Krysta M. Svore, Taylor L. Patti
item.description:
AI agents generate Lean 4 proofs of toric-code Hamiltonian properties and spectral-gap perturbation bounds certifying that a superconducting device Hamiltonian retains the code space.
Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

item.title: Asymptotically Optimal Weighted Edge Colorings via Local Bin Packing
item.dc:creator: Rishikesh Gajjala, Arindam Khan
item.description:
The five upper-bound existence statements for weighted edge coloring are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, AI-assisted, in a companion repository.
We study weighted edge coloring, where each edge of a graph $G$ has a weight in $(0,1]$, and colors are assigned so that the incident weight of each color at every vertex is at most one. The objective is to minimize the number of colors, denoted by $χ'_w(G)$. This generalizes classical edge coloring (all weights are one) and bin packing ($G$ is a star). Two natural lower bounds are the maximum weighted degree $Δ_w(G)$ and the maximum local bin-packing number $\mathrm{bp}(G)$: the maximum, over vertices, of the minimum number of unit bins needed to pack the incident weights. We have $\lceilΔ_w(G)\rceil\le\mathrm{bp}(G)\leχ'_w(G)$. How closely these local lower bounds approximate the global optimum is a longstanding open problem. Our main result establishes an asymptotic weighted analogue of Vizing's theorem: every simple graph admits a coloring using at most $(1+o(1))\mathrm{bp}(G)$ colors. Thus local bin packings can be made globally consistent with asymptotically vanishing relative loss, even in nonbipartite graphs. Our local-to-global rounding framework coordinates feasible local packing distributions into a partial coloring, leaving only $o(\mathrm{bp}(G))$ uncolored weight at every vertex. For bipartite multigraphs, we prove $χ'_w(G)\le(2+o(1))Δ_w(G)$, establishing the Chung–Ross conjecture [SICOMP'91] asymptotically. For loopless multigraphs, we obtain the exact bound $χ'_w(G)\le3\lceilΔ_w(G)\rceil$. Both leading coefficients are optimal, giving weighted analogues of the classical Kőnig–Shannon bounds. Further upper and lower bounds show that the classical factor-$3/2$ separation does not persist with the local bin-packing benchmark. We also disprove the exact weighted-degree conjecture of Feige and Singh [ESA'08]. Our upper bounds have polynomial-time algorithms, and their existence statements are formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: Reap: Uncovering Monte Carlo proof search with a lightweight model
item.dc:creator: Yutong Wang, Xuanzhi Ren, Tianyi Xu, Ruitong Liu, Jingda Xu, Peihao Wu, Bryan Dai, Bin Dong
item.description:
Implements policy-value-guided MCTS proof search as a Lean 4 tactic via Lean metaprogramming, then trains and evaluates a 1.7B prover on Lean benchmarks.
We present Reap, an open framework for learning and analyzing formal proof search in Lean4. Reap implements policy-value-guided Monte Carlo Tree Search directly in Lean, sharing proof-state transitions, AND-OR search, and replay verification between inference and training rollouts. Structured action logs expose how neural predictions and tactic execution interact during search. Using this framework, we train Reaper-1, a 1.7B-parameter policy-value model, through continued pre-training, supervised tactic learning, and iterative search-based reinforcement learning. Using a separate premise selector, the final system solves 79.9% of miniF2F-test at pass@32, establishing state-of-the-art performance among open provers of comparable size while remaining competitive with substantially larger models. Beyond improved solve rates, our results suggest that RL strengthens the prover's ability to organize proofs around useful intermediate results, favoring substantial advances over repeated local adjustments. This more directed proof construction is accompanied by increasingly elaborate tactic programs: fewer explicit search decisions are needed, while more work is performed within each decision. The resulting trade-off between search effort and tactic execution cost provides insight into how learning changes the prover's problem-solving strategy.

item.title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
item.dc:creator: Sreehari Sankar, Debargha Ganguly, Vikash Singh, Mohsen Hariri, Weicong Chen, Yanyan Zhang, Shouren Wang, Wang Yang, Chaoda Song, Alexander Nemecek, Osama Zafar, Idan Davidovich, Yuting Shao, Kai Ye, Biyao Zhang, Xinpeng Li, Joe Stubbs, Erman Ayday, Jing Ma, Vipin Chaudhary
item.description:
Implements a Lean 4 runtime that checks agent tool calls against Lean policies, proves the decision procedure equivalent to LeanLTL semantics, and uses metaprogramming for proof-guided repair.
Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

item.title: Exact Shortest Paths and Maximum Flow in Planar Networks in the CONGEST Model
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Senge
item.description:
Three key lemmas (virtual-source lemma, dual distance lemma for the face-disjoint graph, discretized boosting step) are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, sorry-free.
In the CONGEST model, exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) with nonnegative weights and exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks have both been solved in $\tilde O(D^2)$ rounds, where $D$ is the hop diameter, while the lower bound is $Ω(D)$. Given the approximate distance labels of a recent preprint (arXiv:2606.31192), which we use as a black box, we solve exact directed SSSP in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. It rests on a lemma that answers queries from a virtual source with the labels, and on a corrected discretization of the reduction of exact to approximate distances (arXiv:2210.16351). All further bounds of the form $\tilde O(D)$ and $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ use these labels. Through the reduction of arXiv:2303.00811, SSSP with negative weights, or the detection of a negative cycle, takes $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ rounds with high probability. We weight the face-disjoint graph of arXiv:2411.11718 so that its distances are dual distances, which turns distance problems in the dual into problems in a planar network of hop diameter $O(D)$. This gives exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks in $\min\{\tilde O(D^2),D\cdot n^{o(1)}\}$ rounds with high probability, and in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds with $s,t$ on a common face. In undirected planar networks, the value of a minimum $st$-cut and a minimum cut take $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. For this we repair the auxiliary graphs of arXiv:2608.09500 at $s$ and $t$, and we show that its recursion, as we read it, can miss the minimum cut, also with exact shortest paths: on a network with $11$ vertices it reports $37$ for a minimum cut of $15$. Two more shortest-path computations per level make it exact. The virtual-source lemma, the weighting of the face-disjoint graph and the corrected discretization are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; all other arguments are proved on paper only. Numerical checks are not used in any proof.
